speechtext:
Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved for leave to introduce bill No. 16, to amend the Alberta Natural Resources Act.
He said: The purpose of this bill is to confirm the agreements between the government of Canada and the government of Alberta set out in schedules I and II.

maintopic: ALBERTA NATURAL RESOURCES
subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF AGREEMENTS BETWEEN GOVERNMENT OF CANADA AND GOVERNMENT OF ALBERTA
speechtext:
The agreement in schedule I of the bill provides for the settlement of differences which have arisen between the dominion and the province as to the effect of the natural resources transfer agreement and
Alberta Natural Resources

the ownership and control of three developed power sites on the Bow river lying within or adjacent to the Stony Indian reserve. The three sites known as the Horseshoe, Kananaskis and Ghost sites were developed by the Calgary Power Company Limited and are being operated under authorizations issued by the dominion government in the years 1909, 1912 and 1929 respectively, when they were under exclusive dominion jurisdiction prior to the transfer of natural resources in 1930.
The agreement in schedule I provides that the land and water power at the two sites in which the Indian interest predominates, namely Horseshoe and Kananaskis, are to remain under dominion jurisdiction, while the Ghost site, where the provincial interest is substantial, shall be deemed to have passed to the province at the time of the transfer of the natural resources. The Minister of Mines and Resources will issue all three licences which are to replace the existing authorization and will continue to administer the Horseshoe and Kananaskis developments, while the province will be responsible for administration of the Ghost development as soon as the final licence is issued.

maintopic: ALBERTA NATURAL RESOURCES
subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF AGREEMENTS BETWEEN GOVERNMENT OF CANADA AND GOVERNMENT OF ALBERTA
speechtext:
Under the Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Act, 1930, certain public shooting grounds and bird sanctuaries were preserved. Many of them have now dried up or are otherwise unsuitable for the purposes for which they were originally set aside. The agreement in schedule II provides that these reservations may be cancelled by agreement between the two responsible ministers concerned with the approval of the governor in council and the lieutenant-governor in council
Concurrent legislation by the dominion parliament and the legislature of Alberta will be necessary.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: I will put the question now. In view of the very serious housing situation in the city of Kitchener and other towns and cities throughout Canada, is it the intention of the Department of National Defence to adopt a policy of making military camps throughout the country available for urgent housing accommodation as and when these camps are closed for military purposes? speakeroldname: Mr. HUGUES LAPOINTE (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National ' Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
maintopic: HOUSING
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO USE OF AVAILABLE MILITARY CAMPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member sent to me in the absence of the Minister of National Defence a copy of his question.
The Department of National Defence is doing all possible to render army camps available for civilian housing, subject to continuing requirements of the army for demobilization. The district officers commanding have been authorized in the event of an emergency to place vacant army buildings at

Housing
the disposal of civil authorities. This measure is of a temporary and emergency nature only.
From the long term viewpoint whenever a camp becomes surplus to requirements this department takes immediate steps to declare the buildings surplus to the crown assets allocation committee, which has jurisdiction in the matter of reallocation of accommodation between government departments or agencies or for disposal through War Assets Corporation. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRIORITIES ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
The question I am about to
ask I do not expect to be answered to-day, because I did not have an opportunity to present it to the Minister of Reconstruction before now. It is a matter which has been raised before. I raise it with all deference, because we are receiving so many representations with respect to it. It has to do with priorities on building materials.
As a member of parliament-and I think this applies to all members of the house-I am receiving urgent representations from business concerns, suppliers of building materials and other individuals desiring to build, or to complete construction of, or to repair, their own houses. The chief source of grievance in these representations is that because of priorities in favour of Wartime Housing Limited, bottle-necks are being created in the building trades. The fear exists that unless some early and reasonable modification is made in the present code of priorities, the purpose of their existence will be defeated and will have the effect of shutting off large sections of private enterprise from the building field. In view of the urgency of this matter, I would like to ask the Minister of Reconstruction if not necessarily now but at the earliest possible date, he would make a statement to this house as to the advisability of making some reasonable modification in present building material priorities.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction) :
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: QUESTION AS TO PRIORITIES ON BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
There is a great misconception
about the matter of priorities. In so far as I am aware, there are no priorities in building materials. There seems to be a theory that we have large stocks of building materials frozen or tied up in warehouses.
I received notice a short time ago of a question. The question was not asked, but I had. the answer here. Perhaps it is typical of the situation. The question stated:
Approximately 700 houses now under construction by private persons or contractors of which 174 are for veterans. This is in addition to houses already completed. Meantime materials furnished for Wartime Housing will not be used for some months and are lying in warehouses while houses under construction by private contractors cannot be finished for lack of priorities on materials furnished for Wartime Housing.
That referred to Calgary. The situation was investigated. The situation regarding the Wartime Housing project in Calgary is this: The roofing, shingles, rock wool and mill-work have all been ordered and are in various stages of process and shipment. Four cars of lumber are on hand and sufficient rough plumbing to build the first twenty houses. Concrete is being poured at the rate of four houses per day. There is, therefore, no hold-up in the project, and the material on hand and in process is definitely not too far advanced for the progress being made.
In other words, Wartime Housing orders material for delivery to fit the completion of the work. No stocks of material are being held by Wartime Housing. Wartime Housing
Housing

deals on a mass production basis and buys its material in carload lots, which gives it an advantage over the private contractor. Of course it buys wholesale, which is not particularly popular with the local dealers. It has of course the advantage of building a large number of houses which are constructed from the same plans, and also the large-scale buying of a number of identical articles which arises out of that advantage.
I may say also that it is in the unfortunate position of furnishing an excellent alibi for those who do not plan as well as Wartime Housing in the carrying out of their projects, and of that fact advantage is being taken. I do not think there is a house building organization in this country which has not written me that it cannot carry on because Wartime Housing is building; but I think hon. members will hardly regard it as reasonable that Wartime Housing should modify its procedure on that account.

maintopic: MEAT RATIONING
MEAT RATIONING
subtopic: SPECIAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE OF RETAIL DEALERS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MEAT RATIONING
subtopic: SPECIAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE OF RETAIL DEALERS
speechtext: I have two questions to direct to the ministry on subjects that have been raised before, but which I now with all deference raise again. One is to the Minister of Finance and the other to the Minister of Reconstruction. I would ask the Minister of Finance what changes in meat rationing have been recommended by the retail meat advisory committee, and what is the attitude of the government in respect to these recommendations.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: MEAT RATIONING
subtopic: SPECIAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE OF RETAIL DEALERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can read a statement in reply to the question. It is a bit long and I dislike reading long statements on the orders of the day, but probably there is no help for it.
In replying to the question of the hon. leader of the opposition, of which he was kind enough to give me notice, I .should like to say just a word, in the first place, about the position and function of the wartime prices and trade board's advisory committees. The board has about two hundred voluntary advisory committees across the country with which it consults from time to time on problems relating to their particular sections or levels of a trade or industry. It has always been clearly understood both by the board's officials and by the members of these advisory committees that all discussions and exchanges of views at such meetings are confidential. This is because premature or partial disclosure of suggestions relating to possible changes in board regulations would often be confusing or misleading, and also because the board must necessarily accept full responsibility for all administrative decisions reached.
However, in view of the considerable interest in the house and in the country in matters relating to meat rationing, it may perhaps be regarded as not improper if I make a brief statement in reply to the question asked by the hon. leader of the opposition.
I should like to make it clear that there are four or five advisory committees to the board which have a definite interest in meat rationing, from the primary producer right through to the retail meat dealer. During the past three or four weeks the board has been in renewed consultation with all these committees, and in addition the board has received a great many communications suggesting particular modifications in the rationing system. All the views and suggestions

Meat Rationing
have been carefully considered by the senior officers of the board and by the technical rationing officials.
Among its advisory committees the board has had for nearly four years both a national and regional retail advisory committees, but not a national advisory committee composed solely of retail meat dealers. At the conclusion of its meeting with the large retail meat dealers' delegation on September 19 the board invited the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada to nominate a special advisory committee of representative retail meat dealers with which the board could confer from time to time on matters relating to meat rationing. This invitation was accepted and the first meeting of the committee took place on Wednesday of this week.
I should like to make it clear that this was a meeting of the board and an advisory committee, and not a meeting with a delegation that came to present a case. The nature of the meeting was a review of the system of meat rationing in the light of three weeks' experience, and in the course of the discussions, which lasted through the entire day, many suggestions were made by members of the committee and many practical problems were fully discussed. On some of the points put forward there was fairly general agreement, on others there appeared to be a majority view; still other suggestions appeared to relate more particularly to local situations. And the same kind of discussions took place in the meetings with the other advisory committees mentioned above.
Perhaps the most generally held view among the retailers was that such cooked meats as bologna, weiners, meat loaves and jellied meats should be off the ration. The position of the board is that it is not possible to accept this suggestion and still stay within the target of 130-135 pounds per capita consumption. Under our earlier system of meat rationing two years ago most of these cooked meats were off the ration, with the result that during the ten months of rationing their current rate of production nearly doubled, from an estimated rate of about 100,000,000 pounds a year to a rate of nearly 200,000,000 pounds a year. If these cooked meats were off the ration, the board would have to place rigid and complicated quota controls limiting all production at the source, and would also have to reduce the so-called "red meat" coupon values in order to stay within the over-all meat consumption target. This would be even more objectionable to both the secondary meat processors and the retail trade.
The board is, however, taking steps to revise the coupon values of most of these cooked meats, and assuming that they cannot 47696-51i
be ration free, this appears the most accepts able alternative to all interested sections of the trade.
The next most general subject of comment by the members of the retail committee was that coupon values for some cuts of meat appear not to be accurately matched with consumer buying preferences, with the result that some cuts of meat appear less readily saleable. On these points there appeared to be a considerable variation in actual experience between individual butchers and between districts. Some members reported little difficulty along these lines, others reported a good deal of difficulty.
The board is carefully reviewing all these detailed suggestions, and while it will take a few days to work out the technical adjustments, I am able to say that the board will be making changes in the coupon values of several of these items which will go quite a long way in meeting the consensus of views developed with the retail advisory committee.
I cannot be precise as to the details or as to the date upon which these changes will go into effect. It will take a few days to work out the details, but I am informed by the board that they will be advertised in the press and in effect by the middle or at the latest the end of next week. Reprints of the revised and consolidated ration charts will be distributed as soon as possible, probably within a couple of weeks.
Perhaps I should add a word about the use of "tokens". The decision to make use of tokens was made in the light of very numerous and widespread expressions of opinion by the retail trade and consumers during the rationing period two years ago, when the need for some sort of "small change" for coupons became apparent. While there are some places where the use of tokens still appears to be something of a difficulty, I think it is now reasonably clear that retail meat dealers in most parts of Canada are finding them a very acceptable improvement in the mechanics of rationing.

maintopic: MEAT RATIONING
subtopic: SPECIAL ADVISORY COMMITTEE OF RETAIL DEALERS
speechtext:
I thank the minister
for this very full statement.

speechtext:
Last evening just before the dinner recess I was unavoidably absent from the house when questions were directed to the Minister of Labour. I took note of them, however, and would like to answer them now.
SOi
Labour Conditions

The hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) asked:
Can the Minister of Labour inform this house as to developments in the proceedings with respect to the strike at the Ford Motor Company plant at Windsor, and other threatened strikes ?
My reply is that there is no change in the situation. The union concerned has not altered its attitude towards the company's objection that its officers are not willing to enter a conference with union representatives and the ministers of labour for the dominion and the province, while the union persists in its policy of picketing the main office of the company and preventing its officers and clerical staff from gaining access thereto. The position of the company has been made known to the officers of the union, and the union's reply thereto was transmitted to the company.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) asked:
In view of the gravity of the strike situation at Windsor, will the government or the minister consider the immediate appointment of a controller to take charge of the Ford plant and resume production there pending the negotiation of an agreement between the parties?
My reply is: It is the opinion of the department of labour of the Ontario government, which is in the direct line of responsibility, as well as the Department of Labour of the dominion government, that the plan of bringing the parties together is the one which has the best hope of successful conclusion of the work stoppage.

speechtext:
In answer to that question may I say that I am not in a position to speak on behalf of the naval air service, as it comes under my colleague the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services. He will be dealing with that when he continues with his estimates.
Yesterday the suggestion was made that an over-all statement should be made concerning the three defence services. I should like to point out to hon. members of the committee that the estimates that are before the committee at the present time are very largely made up of expenditures that were incurred during the period of the war, and also expenditures incurred in connection with demobilization. The war has been over only a matter of seven weeks, therefore it will be realized that we have not progressed very far in determining what our post-war organization shall be. The atomic bomb was dropped something like eight weeks ago, and will possibly revolutionize defence forces hereafter. As a result, no very definite programme can be produced at the present time.
On the other hand I can well realize that the committee may want to have before it the defence programmes of the three services before passing on the defence estimates. I regret that the Minister of National Defence was called away yesterday and was therefore unavoidably absent, and is not able to be back to-day. I think it can be arranged for him to go on and complete his naval estimates next Tuesday, and possibly continue on from there to make his report in connection with the army, so that the committee will have before it the programmes of the three defence departments before coming to any final consideration of the estimates for each department.
It was suggested that perhaps the programmes of the defence departments were not carefully coordinated. I want to assure hon. members of the committee that estimates are not prepared in watertight compartments by the departments concerned, and have been correlated before being brought in here. In the first place, programmes are prepared in the various service departments. They are then outlined by the various departmental officials and are subject to revision by the defence council, which has on it representatives of the three defence services. That revised programme for each of the services is then considered by the defence committee of the cabinet, and finally approved by the government. Therefore in that way the appropriations of the three services are carefully considered and balanced before they are presented to the house.

Before we go on to an examination item by item I should like to say a word with respect to the creation of a fleet air arm and to lay before the two ministers concerned, the Minister of National Defence for Air and the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, certain factors which I believe should be considered very carefully before they embark upon any large undertaking in the way of a fleet arm.
I do not propose in any way to oppose the creation of such an arm. The naval air force did credit to itself, to its country and to the allies during the last war, but I think the attention of hon. members should be called to the fact that in creating a fleet air arm we will be creating a duplicate service. My hon. friend the minister may say that I was minister when the fleet air arm was brought into being, and I shall have to admit that my better judgment was coalesced into acquiescing, in the stress and strain of the war and probably because of the glamorous deeds of the flat tops and aircraft carriers of the Royal Navy. But here is what it means, and this was pointed out at the time. In all probability it means a double set of aerodromes, a double set of training schools, a double set of technical schools to train the technical men, a double set of staff officers to plan-and a great deal of planning goes on in the armed services. I notice the hon. member for Cape Breton South in his place. I am sure he and all his socialistic friends would be only too pleased to be members of the staffs of the armed services, because they spend a very great deal of time planning. It would mean a double set of planners and a double set of designers. I think it is fairly well known to hon. members that the design of the aircraft used by the fleet air arm is not the same as the design of the aircraft used by the army,
by the Royal Air Force and by the R.CA.F. There are perhaps reasons why they should differ in certain respects, but I would point out that the most famous raid made during the war, that of Doolittle on Tokyo, was made with army aircraft.
So it goes, all through the piece. But it means more than additional expenditures. I believe I am justified by the experience in the last war in saying that it means a certain amount of rivalry, a certain lack of harmony as between two very great organizations, the navy and the air force. It is not betraying any secret to say that it was notorious in the United States that the United States navy did not get on with the army, and that situation was particularly glaring with respect to their air services. There have been rumours that in Britain the high lords of the admiralty were even a bit sticky; and that the people of the air force, as perhaps befits a young and growing organization, were a bit cocky, so perhaps they did not get along any too well either. In any case Canada had to furnish training schools for the fleet air arm at Kingston, Aylmer, St. Eugene and I think one or two other places.

The R.A.F., because a large number of our men were being trained for the R.A.F. My contention is that if some of the men who had been through their elementary and intermediate stages of training had been taken on and given the last phases of training which would be necessary to make them fleet air arm flyers, it would not have been necessary to begin training all over again. I fear that with two great organizations such as the navy and air force competing for recruits, both endeavouring-and this is a legitimate ambition on the part of those within these services-to build up a better organization, in this country we will have a lack of harmony which will not serve the purpose either of the nation or the forces themselves. So I suggest
Demobilization-Air Services

to the two ministers that before we get into the position of creating this fleet air arm; before the inevitable happens, as it will happen in this house and this country, and people say we are paying too much for the armed forces; before we create a duplicate service; before we do an injustice to those who may very properly embark upon a career in the fleet air arm, by perhaps axing them later on, after a few years, we carefully consider not whether we should have men flying from carriers but who shall be responsible for the organization.
In the last war it was possible for the Royal Air Force and the R.C.A.F. to organize observation units, as I think they were called. Hon. gentlemen who are more familiar with what happened overseas than I am will remember that the army desired to have artillery officers trained as observers. We thought it would be easier to take a pilot who had gone through a year and half or two years of flying training and train him to spot for the artillery than to train an artillery man to fly to the place he wanted to be. The discussion did not last very long, and the army won, but eventually, during the course of the war, those observation units came under the control of the	air force.	So whether it be	the R.A.F. orthe	R.C.A.F.	it seems to	me	it should be
possible to reconcile the training, the supply and the organization of men who will fly from battleships or carriers and men who will fly from the ground, without creating a very expensive organization.
If	I may do so I would	like	to suggest tothe	ministers that they	get	together the
officers of their departments, for there are excellent officers in both departments who know this whole story far better than perhaps anyone in this house knows it. Let them get together and put their cards on the table, because we are starting something new. That was done in the old country after the last war, where there was a controversy which lasted for years. Eventually the big navy people won and a fleet air arm was created; but before embarking on this policy let us give it careful consideration. I think the ministers could discuss it with their officers, and if they cared to have it, there are men in this house who could in an informal way give them all the advice possible. There are men on both sides of the house able to do that. Before any of us get into a controversial argument or wed themselves to a big navy or a navy air arm or a land air arm, let us have all the facts and give them serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, we have all listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just sat down. I am not rising to comment on the subject he raised, but I am sure that with the splendid record he had as Minister of National Defence for Air, this house and the country will listen with respect to the statement he has made.
I am rising for another purpose. It is as to procedure in this committee. There is only the one resolution before us. It is asking that 81,365,000,000 be voted for war expenditures and demobilization. Any member may get up and discuss anything that may be included within the details of that appropriation. It seems to me that unless we arrive at some understanding and discipline ourselves, we may very well talk here for a couple of months. As leader of one party I want to say that we are prepared to discipline ourselves and to confine ourselves to a discussion of individual items when we come to them. However, before that time arrives I think a full discussion of the general situation should be open to any hon. member who wishes to apeak. I feel also after the experience of last night that I should say something more at this time.
The different ministers of defence have been asked to give us an over-all statement of their policy with respect to defence, but up to now such a statement has not been forthcoming. The Minister of National Defence for Air referred to this request to-day, and indicated that he was not in position to make any such statement except for an interim period. A good many hon. members will be disappointed that we have not heard more. However, he said that the Minister of National Defence-army and navy-would be here at a later time and might be able to supplement what he had to say.
Quite frankly when we reached these estimates last night I felt a good deal of frustration. The minister has now indicated that they do not mean that they have been allocated out of the $2,000,000,000 that was voted last year, but that the treasury board has apportioned the amount to each item. Is that correct?

As I remember, last
night the minister intimated that a certain amount had been allocated, first of all for the first item in his estimates. He then went on to say that some treasury board had altered that amount, and that the allotted amount was the figure shown in the first column. What I am getting at is that that column does not mean very much to us. The minister has come along to-day and has given us the expenditures for five months- expenditures for the five months under each of these items. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East, however, that that information is not very helpful to us in considering these estimates.
As I look back over the last half dozen years of war I find that this house granted to the government large amounts of money without much question and without much consideration. Now the ministers are relating the present requirements to the amounts voted in the past. Our position is that these total expenditures increased too rapidly and are not decreasing rapidly enough. In view of the situation in which we find ourselves I should like to say something to-day which I had planned to say on an earlier occasion but which I was unable to say for reasons which the committee will understand.
The resolution before us has to do with war expenditures and demobilization. It asks that we approve the granting to the government of $1,365,000,000 for expenditures on these items over a seven months period. On Friday last the Minister of Finance presented to this house a statement in explanation of his request for this appropriation. When he got through we saw what the total was; in fact it had been intimated before. Since that time many hon. members of this house have spoken, including the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), 47696-52
the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) and others. If I may say so, for moderation and tolerance and non-partisanship I doubt if those addresses have been excelled in this house at any time that I can recall.
A few days ago the Minister of National Defence presented another statement. It was with respect to naval expenditures. When he got through he intimated that he wanted $172,000,000, after indicating that the force would be reduced, if I remember correctly, to 10,000. Yesterday the Minister of National Defence for Air presented his statement in which he indicated that the air force would be reduced to 15,000 or 20,000, and he outlined his idea of what its interim organization should be.
I submit that the government has done itself less than credit in the case it has presented in asking for $1,365,000,000 for seven months. This leads me to deal with one aspect of this measure, the business aspect. The other day the hon. member for Vancouver South dealt with defence policy. He asked for an over-all statement from the government, and he volunteered some constructive suggestions. We are still waiting for that statement. The hon. member for Vancouver South was followed by the members for Lake Centre and Kamloops in criticism of the policy of carrying on, now that the war is over, by order in council under the War Measures Act.
There are four major aspects of the measure now before us to which we might give attention. One is what we might call the remnants of the war expenditures. Another is the welfare of the returning men and of the dependents of those who will not return. The third is defence policy for the future, and the fourth the business aspects of the whole matter. I shall not take more than two or three minutes to refer to the first three.
With respect to the remnants of the war expenditures, obviously our commitments must be met. But in saying that, I think we should also say that unnecessary expenditures and waste must be eliminated. I am sure that the ministers are endeavouring to see that that is done right now. I think also that the huge expenditures of the past should be brought under review, not in closed session, but in open session.
With respect to the welfare of the returning men and their dependents, this has been the subject of earnest consideration by a committee of this house in the past and will

Demobilization-Air Services

be again, as well as in the deliberations of this committee, and I am sure it will receive long and considered judgment by the members. We must try to see that the young men who fought in this war shall not be economically worse off for having done so. Physically they should be restored to the maximum of health that modern medical science can achieve for them. With respect to their adjustment from war-time to peacetime activities, we should see that they are given the training that they missed when they went away, and any additional training we can give them, and that they shall have work suitable to their capacity at reasonable rates of pay on their return.
With respect to the defence policy of the future we shall await a further statement from the government. The member for Vancouver South the other day made some suggestions which received favourable commendation from many sections of the house. Whatever we may decide upon in detail in our plans for the future, I think we must do two things: we must plan to protect ourselves against attack, and we must cooperate fully with other nations to try to see that we are not attacked.
Now I come to the phase of the matter with which I wish to deal in greater detail, the business aspects not alone of this particular measure but of the sum total of them all.
I think at the outset that we should take stock of where we are at to-day. Here we are in the middle of a fiscal year, and we have had no budget-meeting in the middle of the fiscal year with half of a year's money spent without the expenditures having had adequate consideration either by this parliament or the previous parliament; meeting in the middle of the year with civil estimates for six months already passed-five months last winter and one month for which we granted interim supply three weeks ago; meeting in the middle of a fiscal year with wrar estimates for seven months already voted without much consideration-with five months supply voted last winter and $400 million or the equivalent of two months' interim supply voted three weeks ago; and now' here we are meeting in a short session with insufficient time to give to these tremendous expenditures the full consideration they should receive.
It is a most unusual situation. In our judgment, Mr. Chairman, it is an inexcusable situation. It has never happened before, so
far as I have been able to learn. It should not have been allowed to happen now; it must never happen again. There is no reasonable

defence for our being in this position, discussing expenditures that reach the huge sum of $5,000 million a year, over half of which has been already spent.
What does -this measure aim to do? This is the first step in a procedure to make available $1,365 million for seven months for certain purposes. That is a lot of money-$200 million a month-$7 million a day. Since this measure was introduced a week ago $50 million of the Canadian taxpayers' money has been spent under this measure. And that is not all. The civil estimates were laid before us some time ago asking for an expenditure for the twelve months' period of more than $1,000 million. In addition to that there had already been voted last winter the huge sum of $2,000 million for war purposes, making a total of these three items of $4,388 million or the equivalent of some $12 mililon a day. But that is not all either, Mr. Chairman.
At page 565 of Hansard the Minister of Finance indicated that there were other expenditures not included in these amounts. He indicated that there were war service gratuities and reestablishment grants that would amount to $240 million a year, to be added to these other appropriations. On the same page he indicated that export credits and foreign exchange control expenditures would have to be added as well. He did not give the total amount, but he summed up by saying that the total would come to more than $5,000 million for the year in which we now find ourselves.
That figure is large, but it is not all we should be thinking about. What we should be thinking about as well is that this is the people's money we are dealing with, and that when we approve these measures we approve *the taxes necessary to raise the money, and we approve the debts necessary to pay for the deficits. It is important that we should realize the full implications of our action. It is only because I feel that these expenditures, which were increased to such tremendous heights under the patriotic impulse of war, are not being reduced fast enough that I have taken these few minutes to bring out some of these points to-day.
My general criticism of the situation in which we find ourselves may be mentioned under four headings.
The first criticism is the disrespect which has been shown to parliament by letting six months go without a budget, by permitting six months to pass without adequate consideration of these tremendous expenditures, and in bringing us here too late to deal adequately with them. Hon. members know very well the reason. Parliament was called to meet here

Demobilization-Air Services
last January 31. It met one day and prorogued the same day; it was called again for March 19, and sat for four weeks or until the life of that parliament expired; and it ended without a budget and without adequate consideration having been given to expenditures. Now, late in the year, with half the money gone, and very little time left to deal with the matter, we are here and are asked to consider and take responsibility for passing these huge amounts.
The second criticism I want to make, and I make it in all seriousness, is that in the manner of bringing these expenditures before the house the government has removed the most effective check it had upon the prevention of waste. We have before us one resolution asking for $1,365 million. When the civil estimates come down for $1,000 million you will have over four hundred different resolutions. When these resolutions pass, no branch of the service can exceed the amount voted under each item. It has not the power to do it, and the only way the government can get any additional money for any such item is by governor general's warrant. But what do we see here? The government brings in one resolution and has provided us with a breakdown to help us consider the total, but it does not carry the breakdown into the bill; so when we are through, the government for this purpose will have $1,365 million in one lump sum into which hundreds, yes, thousands of officials can dip, and the government is at once put on the defensive. The most effective means the government has of preventing waste has been given up by bringing in estimates in this fashion. The government has forfeited the help which might have come from the heads of five hundred or a thousand sections of the service, in each one of which it would have been some responsible official's duty to see that the expenditures were not increased. But now, everybody is against the government; every service there is will want more money; and in spite of the best efforts of the government its expenditures will be greater than they need be had they been brought forward in the way that ordinary expenditures are brought before parliament.
I realize the answer of the government. In war time nobody raised serious objection to the course it fallowed. But in peace time it ought not to be permitted. I think that is one reason why the expenditures to-day are as high as they are. As I said, under this plan nobody is helping the government to keep the expenditures down. On the contrary, practically the whole public service is against the government. There is perhaps not a service but thinks that its .work is good and wants to 47696-52J
extend it, so the whole pressure of the officials is against the government. Thus, in spite of the government's best efforts, its expenditures will be higher than they need to be.
The government's practice is not in the interest of the minister himself; it is not in the interest of the government; it is not in the interest of the taxpayer.
I have said that the expenditures are unnecessarily high. Let us take a little perspective of what we are doing.
We have no public accounts before this house. The last public accounts available come only to March 31, 1944, and therefore are eighteen months old. That makes it very difficult for hon. members, even if the expenditures of that time were warranted to pass upon these items now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It makes it impossible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
But let us try to get a little perspective of the situation. In the year the war started this government spent $550 million, the next year $700 million, the next year SI,200 million, the next year $1,900 million, the next year $4,500 million, last year $5,300 million. I do not know exactly what it is this year, but the minister indicated the other day that it would be over $5,000 million. Thus the amount in the first year of peace is to be nearly ten times as much as in the first year of war.
Hon. members may not like it; the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) did not like it the other day when I mentioned it; it does not matter; these things must be said. In the last six years this government has spent approximately $20,000 million without adequate consideration by parliament. That is more than was spent by this nation in the whole period of its history up to this war. All of it was spent without any adequate checking up by the government itself or by this parliament.
Because of that huge growth in expenditure, taxes had to be increased. The war-time taxation in 1939 was $300 million, in 1940 $300 million, in 1941 $550 million, in 1942 $1,000 million, in 1943 $1,800 million, in 1944 $2,100 million. I suppose it is even higher this year than it was last year. Last year the total revenue from war-time taxation and other sources was $24,000 million, and that is more than the Canadian people paid in taxes during the first fifty years of the history of this country. Even this large amount paid only half or less than half our total expenditures last year. The balance was raised by borrowing, and how much did we borrow?
In 1939, the year war was declared, the total debt of this nation-in round figures- was $3,700 million, the next year $4,000 mil-
Demobilization-Air Services

lion, the next year $5,000 million, the next year $6,600 million, the next year $9,200 million, the next year $12,360 million. I do not know what it amounted to on March 31 of this year, the end of the last fiscal year, but it probably approached $16,000 million. As that is gross debt, it is not quite a complete picture. Perhaps a more accurate statement of the position is indicated by the net debt, but even that has increased very largely- from $3,100 million in 1939 to $3,200 million in 1940, $3,600 million in 1941, $4,000 million in 1942, $6,200 million in 1943, $8,700 million in 1944, and while we have not been given the figures, it is now probably in the vicinity of $11,000 million. In other words, in these six years we increased our total debt from less than $4,000 million to, I suppose, in the vicinity of $16,000 million, and our net debt from something over $3,000 million to approximately $11,000 million.
The other day the Minister of Finance, in presenting his statement, as reported at page 566 of Hansard, said that interest on the debt, together with one of the social services, family allowances, now came to more than half of the total expenditures in the civil estimates. You have them before you, $1,000 million. The minister said that these two items, interest on debt, and the cost of family allowances, came to half or more of the total figure, or in other words as much as the whole expenditure of the government the year before the war.
I mention these figures, Mr. Chairman, because I think we should have them before us when we are considering what we are going to spend from now on. I want to read two or three extracts from the minister's address in introducing this proposal. The first is on page 548. He says:
It will be noted that this amount-
That is, for war expenditures and demobilization.
-of $3,365,000,000 is $1,085,000,000 less than the total of the war and the Mutual Aid appropriations provided last year.
I do not know exactly why the minister mentioned that reduction. It is true it is a reduction in that item. Later he went on to say that there were almost as many additions to the budget as there were reductions in it. You will find reductions in the estimates for the department of defence for navy, army and air. The figures you will find on page 563 of the minister's address. But I wish to read one other item from the minister's address on page 565.
The amount which we estimate will be required for war service gratuities and reestablishment credits is approximately $240 million

which will, of course, be an expenditure in addition to the appropriation being requested under this resolution.
I simply want to bring together these different items in the government's proposed expenditures so that we can see the total. Further on, on the same page, he said:
To this must be added certain other cash requirements, particularly those for export credits and the financing of the foreign exchange control board which will bring our total requirements for the year above $5 billion.
Or only a little bit short of the total for last year, in this year, the greater part of which is after the war is over. I want to read another statement on the next page. It refers not to this year, which ends next March, but to the year that follows, the year that ends March, 1947.
During the year following this ninth victory loan, and for which it is expected to provide the moneys required over and above our revenues, our expenditures and other cash requirements, including the loans we propose to make to allied nations for reconstruction, will probably amount in all to about four billion dollars.
In the second year after the war is over the government is now anticipating an expenditure of $4,000 million, which is twice as much as in the war year 1942, three times as much as in the war year 1941, nearly eight times as much as in the pre-war years, namely, $3,500 million more than in pre-war days. And that is for the second year after the war is over.
