A little further on the Minister of Finance makes this statement:
In view of these large requirements I believe we must borrow something approaching two billion dollars for this period. This is a huge amount, even though it is much less than the totals we have borrowed in recent years.
And now listen to this. He continued:
Something on this scale is required, however, if the total reduction in our expenditures and cash requirements is not to be reflected solely in our borrowing.
What does that mean? It means that to the extent that they are short they are going to borrow; that in order to make any kind of reduction in taxation they will make it up by borrowing. No other meaning can be read into that statement. In other words, he says that if we borrow enough we can reduce taxation. Mr. Chairman, I have only one comment to make on that, and it is this. In peacetime, to the extent that we depend on borrowing for financing ourselves, we are not

Demobilization-Air Services
facing the issue squarely, and financing on borrowed money is a concession to the well-to-do.
However, the main point I wish to make is that the minister is obviously making it clear now that in order that there may be some reduction in taxation we shall resort to borrowing $2,000 million in the second year after the war is over.
But I must hurry on. In view of the fact that we have had no public accounts since March 31, 1944, I would ask the government to let us have two or three figures. What has been the total expenditure for the fiscal year 1945? There are only three questions; they are very simple. What has been the total revenue from taxation and other sources for the fiscal year 1945? What was the total indebtedness, gross and net, at the end of the fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Ended March 31, 1945?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes. If the record were brought up to date it would be appreciated. The government may or may not be in a position to give it to the present date, but there is no reason why now, many months after March 31, we should not have the figures at least up to that time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I did
not hear the third question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The total indebtedness, gross and net, as at the end of the last fiscal year. I have outlined the situation. It is only a statement of facts. We either continue those expenditures at a very high rate or we reduce them; it is for the house to decide.
In talking about the $4 billion a year expenditure two years after the war is over, the Minister of Finance intimated the other day that about one-third of it would be for what we call the civil estimates. That is more than $1,300,000,000. As I see the picture that faces us, it will not be $1,300,000,000, it is pretty sure to be $1,500,000,000. When the minister intimates that there will be a total expenditure of $4 billion, and says he is to borrow $2 billion, I am wondering if we are not heading for a civil budget approaching $2 billion. When intimations of this kind are given to us I think it is time that we should take into serious consideration where the voting of these huge sums of money is going to lead us.
There is no use in pointing out a situation like this unless one makes some constructive suggestion. I wish to make some. I hope nobody in the government will take offence at them. We have a duty to perform here; we have to present these matters. We are not allowed to help the government to shape
policy; we are not allowed to share with them the responsibility of administration. Whatever other duties we have under the party system, one of them is to try to point out the errors the government is making, and, to make constructive suggestions toward correcting those errors. I have five suggestions I wish to make.
Parliament must meet on time in the future. There is not an hon. member in this committee but realizes that, with the other work the government has brought forward, we have not time to deal with this huge problem effectively.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
May I ask what limits our
time?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The Prime Minister.
M. BRACKEN: Yes, I shall tell you.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
We are prepared to sit here
in this session until next year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: You should have been prepared to come here months ago. As I said, parliament met on January 31 and adjourned the same day, then it did not resume its sittings until March 19, although the government knew that the end of the life of parliament was only four weeks ahead. That was where the first mistake was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
It sat more days last
year than the British parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
It met on March 19 and prorogued on April 16. That is where the first error was made. The second error was made in not getting us here earlier for the session and now there is talk of having another session meeting shortly after the new year, and the idea is to hurry through this one!. No, the mistake was made by the government. There is nothing that we can do now to give us adequate time to deal with these matters.
The second point I wish to make is that there should be no more opening of the public purse for thousands to dip into. That is what this very policy is. When the government brings forward its civil estimates there is not one resolution but 426 or so; and no branch and no department can expend more than the amount that is within each one of these resolutions. The officials in charge of each branch are concerned to see that they do not spend more than that because they have to justify asking for a royal warrant to spend more. All that protection which the ministers and the government have is gone. I sympathize with the government. But its officials are thus all against it. They do not mean to do any harm to the
Demobilization-Air Services

state, but all the state's protection is gone. They are all against you when you should have five hundred or one thousand tried and tested officials there trying to see that these expenditures are not exceeded. By this procedure all that protection is gone.
Nobody raised that question seriously during the war, and I do not raise it too seriously now, although I think in the government's own interest they should have that protection. But I want to give the government fair warning that if it comes forward with requests for these huge amounts in this way next year we shall certainly use all the energy we have to see that it is done in a better way.
My third criticism is that the dictatorial powers allowed the government in war must be taken away in peace. We have had some discussion on that, and I need not go into it in any larger field than what is before us now. It is an easy way for the government to proceed, but it is not an easy way for the government to keep down its expenditures. The government has taken away from itself the best protection it had.
My fourth criticism is that consideration of public expenditures behind closed doors must end.
My last one is that the government must get out of its head that it is a dictatorship.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Oh. oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I know; my hon. friend may laugh. The government did not deliberately plan to become a dictatorship, but when it gets to be one it likes to hang on to it too long. I suppose we would be acting in the same way if we were over there, and if you were over here you would be saying exactly the same thing that I am saying to-day. If you were saying it you would be correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Exactly, we did before.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The time you took the buttons off.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The government must get it into its head that while a democracy will stand for a dictatorship in war, it will not stand for a dictatorship in peace.
We are going to look upon this government as the custodians of the people's money, the people's taxes. As representatives of the people, like any other hon. members, we intend to try to hold the government responsible for its trusteeship, and it is a very heavy responsibility.
I do not propose to keep the committee any longer. I rose to point out where the government's policies have led us. I did not criticize it too seriously during the war, although with proper controls these expenditures could have been kept down then. But I do criticize it when they are not going down fast enough now, and -when from all indications the prospects of getting them down very fast in the future are not bright.
We expect the government to justify these expenditures, and to justify the meagre measure of tax reduction they will bring in because of the size of the expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I do not propose to reply in detail to the remarks of the leader of the opposition, but in the absence of the Minister of Finance I think I should cover one point. He spoke of the requirements for 1947 being $4 billion. The Minister of Finance made it clear, I think, that this is a cash requirement and not a budgetary requirement. It would include the loans which will be necessary to countries that have been traditional customers of ours, particularly the United Kingdom, France, Belgium, Holland, Norway and our sister dominions. A period will be required before the Bretton Woods agreement can go into effect, and before the international monetary fund can come to the rescue of the financial difficulties in converting currency as between one country and another. In that period we contemplate having to finance purchases in Canada of foodstuffs and other materials for these countries. The cost of such purchases is a cash requirement, but it is not a budgetary requirement. Naturally the money so furnished will be a debt owing by these countries to Canada, just as the bonds that will have to be sold to provide the cash to make the purchases will be a debt owing by Canada to the people of this country who will be the owners of the bonds. I believe that distinction should be made, because I should not like any hon. member to think the budget for 1947 will be $4 billion or anything approaching that sum.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister
would permit me a question. Does he really expect that these credits or advances, or whatever they are, will be repaid?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I certainly do.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Louder.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I asked if the minister really expected that these credits or advances would be repaid, any more than the advances under Mutual Aid were repaid. He replies that he certainly does. I doubt if anyone else in the house will give that answer to the question.

Demobilization-Air Services

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I am sorry my hon. friend takes such a pessimistic view of the future of the United Kingdom and the great powers of Europe. Mutual Aid was a gift, and there was never any suggestion of a loan or of any repayment in that connection. The first billion dollars provided for aid to Britain was called a gift and was passed as such by this house. Other money was provided in the form of Mutual Aid, which meant that Britain would pay to the extent of her ability, and that the balance would be a gift. That was made clear to the house. Those moneys will not be repaid. To-day, however, we are making loans which call for repayment to several countries. All these are countries which have paid their debts through the ages; and this applies between Canada and the United Kingdom. I cannot be as pessimistic as my hon. friend, if he suggests that the debts now being incurred by these countries will not be repaid. If we take that attitude, I think we must take the view that the, world can never recover from this war.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I fully agree with one thing said by the leader of the opposition this afternoon. During the several years we have been discussing these war expenditures under a resolution and a bill I have suggested from time to time that we should follow the practice we adopt in connection with our other budgets and estimates; that is, attach to the bill a schedule which would limit the appropriations to the items approved. I understand the difficulties in that connection, and when this method was discussed with the Minister of Finance earlier I reiterated the objection which was raised this afternoon by the leader of the opposition and urged that as soon as possible we should get back to the normal way of doing business and see to it that the estimates were brought down in the usual way both for ordinary expenditures and for what we now term war or demobilization expenditures. I think the argument that has been advanced this afternoon, that the limitations placed upon the departments and officials by the house when the method suggested is adopted, is a valuable safeguard both to the government and to this parliament. We know there are difficulties at the present time, and for that reason we have been inclined not to press the matter during the war years. But now that we have emerged into the peacetime era I think the sooner we get back to the normal way of budgeting our estimates, the better it will be not only for the country but for the government itself.
The other day the Minister of Munitions and Supply said it was planned again to set up the war expenditures committee, to deal with war expenditures and war assets; and I believe that should be done as soon as possible.
I think these expenditures should be very carefully examined. The public accounts committee has a different function to perform; it is more concerned with the ordinary civil estimates and expenditures. I do not think there should be any further delay in establishing the committee to which the minister referred and which during the war we have always called the war expenditures committee, in order that we may go into the criticisms that are heard across the country, although sometimes I feel sure, unjustifiably, from what I know of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. The disposal of our war assets properly comes into a discussion of this kind, because those war assets account for a very large percentage of the money with which we are now dealing. In that connection I have just received a telegram which indicates the misgiving or alarm which some of our people are feeling. I should like to place on record this telegram, which comes from Toronto, Ontario, and reads:
Whereas the Ontario Federation of Agriculture is greatly concerned to hear that the federal government is planning to dispose of the nitrate plant at Calgary to private interest and contrary to proposals submitted by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture it is urged that no action be taken by government until a further meeting with the Canadian federation at which time full disclosure as to costs, markets, benefits to Canadian agriculture, etc., is made and future action planned.
That is signed by V. S. Milburn, secretary of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, and I take this opportunity to bring it to the attention of the minister. There we have a concrete example. We have made very large industrial expenditures for war purposes, and many of our people are anxious that this house should protect the interests of the country to the greatest possible extent. Where we can use these new establishments for the benefit of the Canadian people they should be so used.
May I say just one other word along the line of what the minister was saying a few moments ago. The Minister of Finance has stated that the $4,000 million is a cash requirement. We know perfectly well that a large part of that amount will have to be used either for Mutual Aid or for loans, as the minister has said. I am quite sure the people of Canada realize that while we can set up all the security councils we like; while we can
Demobilization-Air Services

do everything possible in the way of rearmament among our own nations, still we may not obtain the security the world needs if we allow any of the nations who have been our partners in this war to sink into the mire of want and poverty. I believe the large amount involved this year in the way of loans to potential customers, to our allies during the war, will receive support throughout the country, whatever may be involved in the way of borrowing or taxation or other means of raising the money. But before the house is asked to go ahead and confirm these tremendous expenditures which have been made and are proposed, I believe the war expenditures committee should be set up and hon. members given an opportunity in public to go into all items of past expenditure. That is what the committee should do. Then as soon as possible we should return to the old method of going into the budget proposals item by item, having the details of our expenditures attached as a schedule to any bill or bills that may be required. As soon as possible we should provide for expenditures in the normal way, in order to protect this house, this country and indeed the government itself.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Without wanting to be accused of diverting the trend of the discussion, I should like to propound a question to the minister. This has to do with the control exercised at the moment by the R.C.A.F. over civil aviation. Just praise has been given to the work done by the Canadian air force and the commonwealth air training scheme, but aniy one who has read the history of aviation knows perfectly well that had it not been for those good citizens who kept aviation to the fore during the days of peace, who pioneered, shall I say, and laid the basis for the commonwealth air training scheme, the great success which was accomplished during the war by our air forces and the air forces of other countries might not have been so great. There are men on the Pacific coast who are anxious to enter into civil aviation, but information has reached me to the effect that at the moment the R.C.A.F. has direct control over civil aviation. Has the minister given consideration to this question of control by the R.C.A.F. on the Pacific coast and in other parts of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Civil aviation comes under the Department of Transport. Perhaps the Minister of Reconstruction could speak with regard to the hon. member's question.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Information has come to me that these boys have to receive permission 
from the R.C.A.F. in order to be permitted to fly so many miles over and around the airports.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The
R.C.A.F. would have control over the R.C.A.F. airports, but they do not control the activities of civilian flying clubs or civilian flying associations. That would be under the Department of Transport.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
there are only one or two references that I intend to make, one having to do with the statement by the leader of the C.C.F. that he thought a committee similar to the war expenditures committee should be set up. It was indicated the other day by the Minister of Munitions and Supply that it was the intention of the government to bring in a motion to establish such a committee. I speak now for myself, but I think I speak also for those on this side of the chamber when I say that if such a committee is to be set up, the day of secrecy is over as far as we are concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: And the necessity too.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I am glad to have the concurrence of the minister in that regard.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Perhaps the war will be over some day.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I am glad to have the assurance of the Minister of National Defence for Air that when this committee is set up, the question of security no longer arising, there will be no longer any justification for that committee sitting behind closed doors.
The other day when certain questions were placed on the order paper the Minister of Munitions and Supply asked that they be allowed to stand because this committee was to be set up. Let me say that I do not believe this country will consider that the setting up of a committee can be taken as a substitution for the responsibility of the minister to answer in this house for the activities of the War Assets Corporation. In other words, whether or not a committee is set up, we retain our rights to scrutinize thoroughly, by the means of proper questioning, what has taken place in connection with the War Assets Corporation "and to disposal of assets and plants. I notice the minister is laughing. He always laughs when any question is raised as to the necessity of his accounting to parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I just said that the hon.
gentleman should pay an entertainment tax if he wants both.

Demobilization-Air Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
What was the
observation?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I just said that if the hon.
gentleman wants to be entertained in two sessions he should pay an entertainment tax.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
What that means
I do not know and I doubt whether the minister does.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
My hon. friend attempted to
interpret what I said and I told him what I said.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I always listen to
the minister courteously and do not interfere at all, but for some reason, whenever there is an assertion on the part of anyone on this side of the chamber that he as one of the ministers is answerable to this house and to this parliament, he immediately resents it and commences to make remarks similar to the one he has just made.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
On a question of privilege,
I do not resent it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Last evening the
hon. member for Nanaimo asked for an overall plan. That over-all plan was not given, nor has there been any endeavour to give such a plan to the committee. Dealing with the post-war plans, the minister made this statement, as reported on page 765 of Hansard:
No definite decision has yet been made as to the strength and composition of the post-war air force, as until the nature and extent of any commitments that we may have under international or regional agreements have been determined it is obviously impossible to reach any final decision.
First, the minister very pertinently used the words, "no definite decision," and again, that awaiting this definite decison, no "final decision" could be made on the part of the government. I wonder if the minister is in position to place before the committee and the country what the intention of the government is with respect to the contribution that Canada will make, first, to the common defence within the British commonwealth of nations. Have there been negotiations between Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom with respect to the setting up of a British commonwealth air force or the continuation of the British commonwealth air scheme in the days of peace? Have there been negotiations among the various component parts of the empire which may lead to the setting up of a composite air force to be available in the event that war should break out?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
There
have been no such negotiations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
As I understand
the situation arising out of the united nations agreement, Canada's contribution in the main will be an air contribution. Am I correct in that? I understand that the present plans of the government are that Canada's responsibilities under the charter will, either definitely or in substance, be an air contribution. Is the minister in position to answer that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I have
no idea what contribution Canada may be called upon to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: If I may be allowed to interject, I think it has been made quite clear that the reason we cannot prepare a comprehensive plan at this time is that Canada's obligation under the united nations security charter is undetermined. As soon as these obligations are known-and I assume they will be known within the next several months-we shall be able, I think, to announce our peace-time position.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Has any tentative plan been made? The reason I ask is that only the other day the high commissioner for Canada, speaking in Australia, was reported to have said that the Canadian government with a view to uniting Australia, New Zealand and Canada closer together purposed at the earliest possible date to establish an air service between Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Was he correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is civil aviation. I think that is rather outside the point.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Was he correct in that statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes, it has been announced that the plans of Canada for post-war civil aviation include a service between Canada, Australia and New Zealand. But that is not a matter of defence; it is civil aviation. The structure of the post-war security council was laid at Dumbarton Oaks and was further discussed in San Francisco, but my hon. friend will appreciate that the respective responsibilities under the charter have not been determined. At least that is my understanding.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I quite agree. My question was simply this: Are there any tentative arrangements among the different part-s of the empire as to the contribution which the various parts of the empire may make to such a scheme? Has anything been determined along that line?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
No.

Demobilization-Air Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: So that what Canada's contribution will be toward world peace so far as the air force is concerned has in no way been determined, either officially or unofficially?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction; Minister of Munitions and Supply
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: There is one other matter I should like to bring up at this time. It has to do with repatriation. The minister gave the figures last evening of the number that had been repatriated, 37,907 since V-E day. In the last few days-and I think this applies to most members of the house- letters are being received from our men overseas strongly objecting to the slowness of repatriation. Only to-day I received a letter in which the writer, a responsible man overseas in the armed forces, points out that there is a strong feeling of resentment among the armed forces overseas at the delay in repatriation. He states that during the last few weeks there has been an acceleration of repatriation on the part of the Americanis whereas, so far as Canada is concerned, within the last few days the men overseas have been advised that not only will the rate at which repatriation has taken place within recent weeks be diminished but that the bulk of repatriation has been hoisted for a period of eight weeks.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: In order to make the rates relatively equal.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is not what the men overseas think. The men overseas feel that the rate of repatriation planned for the next eight weeks is such that there is unfairness to Canada in the allotment being made by the united nations' shipping pool. They have been advised that during the next month there will be available only two small ships for repatriation purposes. I bring this matter up at this time because two or three letters I have received are dated within the last few days and they all indicate a strong feeling of resentment. I would ask the minister to advise the committee just what is being done to ensure that Canada's share of the shipping available for repatriation is a fair one and that this feeling of resentment on the part of the men will be entirely removed at the earliest possible day by an official statement from the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The shipping which is allotted to Canada to bring our service men and women home is dependent upon the allied shipping commission. The matter of repatriation is handled by the army, which allots space on the ships to the air force. The air force has been allotted its quota every month. We have received our

fair share and are continuing to receive it. The number of air force personnel to be brought back from April to June, according to the programme that was drawn up, was 15,001, and from July to September, 20,602, or a total of 35,603. That was the programme. Actually we brought back 37,907. From October to December next the number projected is 9,000; January to March, 9,239; June and July 1,496. In addition, those who were employed with our 8th Bomber squadron, came back by air. That was an additional number.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: How many of all services are to be brought back in October?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I do not know. The figure I have given is for the air force, and that is the quota allotted. It has been worked out on a fair basis and as long as the shipping remains available those are the numbers we expect will be coming to this country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The hon. member for Quebec South advanced some very sound arguments in support of the contention which was made here the other day that we should be given a clear statement regarding national defence policy. While I realize perfectly well that it is impractical for the government to tell us their final policy over a long period after the war, yet from what has been said this afternoon it is quite evident that Canada will have to stand very much on her own during this interim period. The allotment of commitments to the different nations has not yet been made. Therefore I submit that it is of great importance that during this interim period we should be coordinating our own services for defence. However, I know that we shall not get such a statement from the ministry and I do not intend to labour the point.
The Minister of National Defence for Air was unable or unwilling when this debate started to say whether the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services was going to establish a fleet air arm. Might I ask the Minister of National Defence for Air whether he has included in these estimates any funds for personnel, aircraft or equipment of the Royal Canadian Air Force which might be serving on any carriers with the Canadian navy, should the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services provide such ships?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: No such expenditures are included in the air estimates for the year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the last hour three hon. members have spoken about setting up the war expenditures committee. The only reproach that was made of

Demobilization-Air Services
the war expenditures committee which sat from 1941 to 1944 was that it sat behind closed doors. Perhaps a little history of the war expenditures committee would enlighten certain members who were not in the last parliament.
In 1940 the acting leader of the opposition, Mr. Hanson, suggested in the house that we follow the example of the British parliament in setting up a national committee on expenditures and that we follow as closely as possible the procedure in the mother country. In 1941 the committee was set up, composed, I believe, of twenty-four members divided among the different groups. When they met they decided to follow the practice of the committee in Britain, which always sat in camera. The reasons given were reasons of security and that, if the sittings were held in public, revelations might be made which might give comfort to the enemy. Those were the two reasons advanced for sitting in camera.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I think the minister will agree that only the government members on the committee approved that procedure.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The hon. member for Cumberland in 1941 was a member of that committee. It was subdivided into three subcommittees, and I do not recall that the hon. member absented himself from the sittings, although we had adopted sittings in camera. He regularly attended the meetings and was very helpful.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is very true, but I did so under protest.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I know the opposition would not admit that we were right in taking that decision. They did protest. But they will also notice that what was said before those subcommittees was, in many instances, of a secret nature. We spoke of production, of what we were doing in munitions and supply; we got details from every branch of that department. We studied the three service departments; we discussed pay and allowances and the procedure of the service departments. We even got information as to numbers, formations, and all that. I am still convinced that we were right in hearing evidence of that kind in camera. Those sittings were held to give information to hon. members with a view to reporting to the house and to the government.
I myself do not like the procedure of sitting in camera, but during wartime I thought it was in the best interest of the state to do so. If a committee on war expenditures were set up this session. I agree with the hon. member
for Rosetown-Biggar that the sittings should be public and that all these expenditures should be inquired into and investigated. I do not believe there is anything to hide, or that any harm has been done. There would be at this time no reasons of security. I did not hear the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar complain about the sittings being in camera when meetings of subcommittees were held. Both of us were members of those subcommittees.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Just on that, I did. My view was that there were certain occasions on which a subcommittee had to sit in camera, but otherwise the proceedings should be open. That was the view I expressed throughout.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
We did, if you recall, meet that objection because one of the subcommittees sat openly. I recall that the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) was a member of that committee. He refused to sit on it unless the meetings were public, and that subcommittee sat publicly. It was dealing with questions which did not affect the security of the state or information which would give aid and comfort to the enemy.
As to the setting up of the future committee, I believe the government agrees with what has been said. But I resent aspersions on the former committee. Hon. members sat for three years in and out of session on that committee. They gave valuable time to it; they acted from national and patriotic motives and I really resent suggestions from certain hon. members that the work was not useful or was not well done. I was a member of that committee from 1941 to October, 1942, when I joined the government, and no better group of men could have assembled to study seriously what was taking place and what expenditures were being made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I do not think anybody suggested that the committee did not do good work. I believe it did good work, and I am willing to say so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that from the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. But when the assertion is made that we did not sit in the open to consider these matters, I must point out that certain information could not have been given had our proceedings not been in camera. I do not think hon. members should criticize that procedure. They themselves are aware that we could not let the people know exactly what was taking place in the armed services or in the Department of Munitions and Supply.
Demobilization-Air Services

Some of those who served on that committee are not now members of this house, and I wish to pay tribute to them for the time and. energy and talents which they devoted to that task.
Since this is a new house, and we are not in war time, even though it has not been so legally declared, I hope that the hon. members who will constitute that committee will do as good work as was done in time of war by those of the past parliament. I was so pleased at being on that committee and seeing how it was run, and finding that the government was doing its utmost to protect the public treasury, that were I not a minister I would insist upon being on the next war expenditures committee. I have no doubt it can do useful work and let the public know exactly what we have done with public moneys throughout the year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I wonder whether
hon. members, who have now had a pretty good discussion, will agree to take the items up as they appear in the list which has been distributed. I think we would make better progress if that were done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Before that is done may I ask one question. The minister said yesterday that he could not give any definite or long-term decision as to the size or composition of the air force. That of course is quite understood. But he did say that it would consist of about ten squadrons and about fifteen to twenty thousand men. Will the minister state now on what principles and for what purposes the figure of ten squadrons and fifteen to twenty thousand men was decided? Why, for instance, is it not fifteen squadrons, or five squadrons?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I did not say those were definite figures. I said we were planning on that basis. We are planning on the basis of what has been recommended by the advisers of the department as a balanced force, a force which would be capable of being extended in time of necessity in order to produce a strong offensive force and a defensive force. At the same time we would have in this country the nucleus of a force which would at all times be available if its services should be required at the time of attack, should this country be in the unfortunate position of being attacked. That is the basis on which the matter is being worked out.
I might say further that, under the programme which is being considered-it is not yet definite-the only expenditures for new planes will be on those in the nature of 
transport planes. We realize that it is necessary to have adequate transport planes. The type we are ordering and hope to secure is the new C-54. No steps are being taken at present to secure new bombers or fighters. It is felt that we have large stocks available which have been in service in this war. There will undoubtedly be very rapid developments in that type of aircraft, and while experiments and research are going on in those fields we do not consider it advisable to commit ourselves to the purchase of large numbers of either fighters or bombers, but believe rather that we should continue for the present with those we have available. These, of course, will also be available for the auxiliary squadrons as they are formed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I agree with you that to take the estimates item by item is perhaps the only way in which they can be disposed of. One might talk a long time on the thought-provokers which are on this sheet of paper which has been distributed. But I merely rise to ask a couple of questions which I do not think I could relate to subjects that are on the paper. Before I do that I should like to say that I listened with great interest to the leader of the opposition, particularly a statement that we spent more money the last six years than we had spent in the whole history of the country previously. While he was saying that I was thinking that, regardless of that fact, it did not affect the standards of living of the Canadian people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It is going to, though.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Their standards of living were much higher than they were from 1930 to 1939. If government spending affects the economy of the country in this way it is not a bad idea to continue to spend government money. That could be elaborated on; it is merely a thought. The criticism that the money we have spent in the last six years affected the welfare of the people of Canada is not valid.
Second, the observation was made that we paid more taxes than we did in the previous fifty years. That, too, is an indication that the people had an income and were able to pay taxes. The fact that we were not paying taxes in the previous fifty years is an indication that we were a poor nation and had nothing with which to pay taxes. I hope that we continue to give the people purchasing power so that they may be able to pay taxes and advance the services of the country.
With respect to the national debt, it does not worry me at all. The only thing that worries me about the national debt is the interest we pay on it. The debt accumulated during the war should be free. There should

Demobilization-Air Services
be no interest on it. No one should sit back in a bond house or in a bank and extract interest out of blood money, because that is what it was. Investment in war should not bear interest but should be interest free. In my opinion, the hundreds of Canadian boys who laid down their lives have paid the bill, and when the war is over, the debt should be cancelled. There is no reason why when they come back and go into overalls, into plants and factories, they should start to pay tribute by way of interest to people who sat back comfortably and secure and invested their money. The national debt, apart from the interest, we owe to ourselves. It is not a liability but an asset.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Will the hon. member permit a question? Does he think that the soldiers, sailors and airmen who invested their money in war bonds should not receive interest on them when they come back?
Mr. GIiLLIS: The amount of money the soldiers, sailors and airmen invested is so small-

What about the war
workers?

speechtext: They are not worrying about it either. The war workers are not worrying about it. The soldier who was drawing the large sum of $1.50 a day-

speechtext: One hundred dollars is a lot to him.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR

-had a lot of money to
invest in war bonds. That is only an alibi; it is not an argument.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
What about the war
workers?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
So that the whole story with
respect to the debt accumulated, and the moneys spent, as far as I am concerned, does not ring on me.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is the reason why you will never be in the government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: That is all right. We may be there a lot sooner than you will. What I rose to say, Mr. Chairman, was this. There are two categories within the Canadian air force who in my opinion did not receive just treatment during the war. The first is the Canadian nationals serving in the R.A.F. A considerable number of Canadian nationals went to the old country prior to 1939 and became members of the R.A.F.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes. The question I should like the minister to answer is this. As regards Canadian nationals returning to this country who served in the R.A.F. during the war, are they entitled to the Canadian' gratuity and all the rehabilitation rights to which the R.C.A.F. are entitled? That is the first question. I think they should be. Second, we had. I understand, about five thousand R.C.A.F. personnel who were radar mechanics, and they served, mostly with the R.A.F., in practically every theatre of war. They were also largely isolated. During their period of service with the R.A.F. those boys were denied promotion. The Canadian government instituted, I understand, what was known as shadow promotion. They were promoted to the ranks that they would have held ordinarily if they were with the R.C.AE., but in the R.A.F. they were not allowed to put up their stripes, badges or insignia. During the period in which the radar personnel were with the R.A.F., when shadow promotion was granted, were they paid for their rank? I understand that this shadow promotion was discontinued in 1943. If it was, I think it was an injustice, because I do not believe there was a section of the R.C.A.F. that was under a greater handicap than the radar boys, who served largely as individuals on isolated stations with the R.A.F. groups. They should have been allowed to carry their rank and they should have been paid on that basis. If it was discontinued in 1943 it should not have been, and I suggest that the government should reinstate it and pay those boys for whatever rank they would have had ordinarily were they members of regular R.C.A.F. squadrons. I should like the minister to answer these questions because I do not see anything on the order paper whereby I might be able to relate this matter to a specific item.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: With regard to the question concerning Canadian nationals in the R.A.F., there were a large number who went over and joined the R.A.F. prior to the war, and throughout the war a large number of Canadians were serving with the R.A.F. A considerable number decided to transfer to the R.C.A.F. and they were permitted to do so up until a certain date. It was published in orders as to the date when transfers would cease.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The minister will pardon me, but many of them could not be got in touch with, those far away on the Pacific ocean. Are they barred now from transferring?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Where
there were special circumstances such as those, extensions have been made. A large number
Demobilization-Air Services

did transfer to the R.C.A.F., but that is not the point. The rehabilitation benefits provided by Canada apply to Canadian nationals, those who were citizens of this country prior to the war. I am not sure of the exact date, but I think those who left Canada from 1936 on and served in the British forces may, on returning to Canada, if they return within six months of the date when they are demobilized -I am not tying myself down to whether these terms are the date at which the individual was demobilized or the date of the ending of the war, but within a fixed period-may be entitled to the difference between the Canadian benefits and any benefits they have received while serving with that allied force. So that Canada is looking after those Canadians who have served in the allied forces.
As regards the radar men, I have the greatest sympathy for that group and I agree very largely with what the hon. member has said about them. Early in the war we enlisted in this country the finest type of young men, men with scientific training, and got them into the radar branch. They continued in that branch and were scattered all over the world, operating radar stations throughout Europe and Africa, and they had very little promotion. The work that they were doing was not work that called for promotion. The result was that brilliant young men who joined early in the war, and who, if they had waited and gone to other branches, might have received greater promotion and even commissions, remained leading aircraftmen. I realize that they have suffered a hardship. On the other hand, they have done magnificent work. While I feel that they have been unlucky, yet they certainly have done a magnificent job.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
They should not be
allowed to be unlucky.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: The work they were doing was not work that called for the service of men of higher rank.

A radar man away up
on a remote island certainly deserves some consideration.

regard to shadow promotion, I never heard of it. It might have been brought in and discontinued in 1943. I shall be very glad to make inquiries concerning it to find out when it was brought in and when it was discontinued.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I do not wish to delay the committee unduly, nor do I wish to open up a discussion on the war expenditures committee. The Minister of Public Works said that the only complaint against the war

expenditures committee was that of secrecy. We should have the record cleared up in that regard. I do not mean to say that the war expenditures committee did not do good work, but I do mean to say that there were many objectionable features in connection with it. The members of the opposition who sat on that committee did object to sitting in secrecy. While we had that objection, we did sit on it and we were very glad to do the best fve could in the circumstances. But the objections were more than the mere matter of secrecy. The objections were that in the war expenditures committee matters were dealt with in secret that did not warrant any secrecy whatsoever. I give as an illustration wartime housing and the operation of government corporations. They were dealt with. If the enemy heard all that went on in connection with these matters they would not , have heard anything of value. Then there was the inquiry into the price of boots and the purchase price of property and land. The evidence was given in secret before the committee. Even some of the evidence in connection with those inquiries was guarded by the departmental officials and was sometimes refused to members of the committee. I might also mention that members of the committee complained in the house that copies of the evidence were not supplied to members for their own personal use while they were sitting on the committee. Oh, there were many difficulties.
The Minister of National Defence for Air and the Minister of Public Works have gone farther than the promises made by the Prime Minister a few days ago in saying that the committee that will be set up will not sit in secret. I hope that they will take the matters I have mentioned into consideration too, and that when the committee is set up, not only will it not sit in secret but it will give the evidence untrammeled and unhampered by department officials. I urge that at this time.
I could go into a long discussion on this matter, but I do not wish to delay the committee. However, I believe that the people of Canada want a much closer scrutiny of and much more information on war expenditures than they have had in the past. I believe that the people of Canada feel that in the war expenditures committee many things were discussed in secrecy that had no right to be so discussed or investigated. The people want more information than was given to them in the past because of the secrecy.
When the new committee is set up to investigate war expenditures I hope no attempt will be made to have it sit in

Demobilization-Air Services
secret. There were other objections to the war expenditures committee of the past three or four years. I sat as a member of that committee for a year. I enjoyed it. I appreciated the energy and the efforts of the members of the committee, but I did not appreciate the little attention that parliament was allowed to give to their findings or to the total absence of discussion of the committee reports in the house. When this new committee is set up I hope that these objections will be kept in mind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I hope that the members will now agree to take up the items connected with the department.
Mr. MaeNICOL: Show me the item on which I can ask further questions about the radar boys and I shall be quite satisfied to deal with the items.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Before proceeding with the items I should like a little better understanding of what this money will be used for. What proportion of these estimates will be regarded as demobilization expenses and what proportion will be used for the interim force? Can the minister answer that question?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Some of the items can be broken down in the manner suggested. What is being spent on demobilization can be broken down, but what is being spent on the interim force cannot be broken down into that force entirely. The interim force will consist partly of the occupational force in Germany and the occupational force in other places. It will consist partly of the force employed in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: When will demobilization be considered completed? What time will the interim force come into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I cannot give the committee the date on which demobilization will be completed. According to the plan it will not be completed by March 31, 1946.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I have listened with a good deal of attention to the discussion and the questions ever since the war appropriation measure first came before us. One thing has impressed me as being singular, namely, that no member of the opposition has commended the government for the effort which apparently it is making to maintain a considerable force of fighting men and equipment in Canada in case of an emergency.
I should like to draw the attention of the hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party to the fact that it was their attitude between 1930 and 1935 which reduced the meagre defence of Canada to an intolerably and dangerously low level. This cheese-paring attitude, this worrying about the dollar, will start a similar attitude again in Canada.
I do not wish to be an alarmist; I wish to be a realist. Will any hon. member in this committee, if he asks himself the question honestly and sincerely, dare to say that the era we are now entering is an eara in which we can feel that we are safe? This is an exceedingly serious matter. I am not saying for a moment that all the money has always been spent wisely. I would say this, however, not desiring to commend the government over much, that all things being considered the government in going through this war is to be strongly commended for the high degree of efficiency and effectiveness which it attained at the price that had to be paid for it. When we want defence in this country we want it badly. We are likely to want it again, and that before very long; but whether or not that should be so it is a right, good, safe principle to keep your powder dry and be sure you have plenty of it.
I should like to encourage the ministers who are in charge of the exceedingly difficult departments of defence to do everything that lies within their power to keep the defences of this country at the very highest possible standard consistent with the conditions of the times through which we are passing. The money will be found. I notice plenty of evidence that our Conservative friends are still suffering from a money mentality. How long is it going to take them to realize that the power of the nation to fight, or to prepare to fight, or to do anything else, depends upon the productive power of the nation, the amount of goods and services it can produce? Money is merely a bookkeeping system to represent the capacity of the nation to produce and use goods and services. Does anyone in Canada think for a moment that we are less able to produce goods and services to-day than we were a year ago, or two years ago, or three years ago? Then the degree of defence of which we are' capable in this country certainly must depend upon the degree of production of which we are capable. As soon as we look at this whole matter from that angle we begin to see how unwise it is to emphasize dollars when the very existence of this nation and this empire of which we form a part might be threatened at any time; when all we have won
Standing Committees

and saved through the centuries of our history, including what we have won and saved in this war and the last one, might be lost because we have been indiscreet in the matter of taking precautions against eventualities.
